Friday, october 17, 1952.
Flying Bangkok - Hong Kong.
Dear Girls, Family and Friends:
Well at Bangkok we're starting homeward because that is approximately ecui-distant
from New York whether one travels in an easterly or westwardly direction. To give
you a running (or rather flying) account of our movements since our last letter.
I left New York on the 12th joined Debby in Paris on the 13th and reunited we left
there on the evening of the 13th flew down the Rhone Valley and on to Rome where
we arrived early in the morning of Tuesday, October l4th, to go on after refeuling
to Beirut for breakfast. There we transferred from my New York Boeing double
decker to a DC-6 and climbing high over Beirut cleared the mountain range behind it
to fly over Damascus and on across the vast sands of Saudi Arabia to Basra. The
latter is on a river several miles up from the top of the Persian Gulf as so many
ancient cities its founders had a profound respect for pirates or sea raiders. Most

on a Japanese
passport. In the attack on Hongkong he was imprisioned for the first
few days by the British then released he drove an ambulance for them until the
Japanese took over. The Japs let their "fellow citizen" go to Macao and some months
later, through the good offices of an old Portuguese friend of ours and a sizable
bribe it was arranged for him and two American PAA Macao staff to pass through the
Japanese lines into China. There he hitchhiked and walked his way with his American
friends to a city with an airport and telegraph station. CNAC picked them up and
flew them to Calcutta where he helped CNAC on its operations over the Hump until the
war ended. Then he rejoined PAA as Station Manager -Delhi. Now by virtue of his

years of residence in Hongkong and India he has become an English citizen, married
a most attractive White Russian refugee from Tientsin and seems quite content.
We left Delhi late at night on the l4th passed through Calcutta and arrived Bangkok
early in the morning of Wednesday October 15th. So leaving New York at 7 PM Sunday
Losing 12 hours by flying east, I still arrived half way around the world too early
for breakfast on Wednesdey morning.
We were a little disappointed in Bangkok. Perhaps it wes because the Hotel
Trocadero was a little more
shabby and nothing worked with a greater degree of
regularity than formerly. Perhaps it was because the streets were full of mud in
addition to their customary disrepair. Maybe it was because the night noises were
nearer a 100% din than erstwhile. Whatever it was we left this morning with no
regrets and the firm conviction shared by most visitors that Bangkok needs a first
class hotel.
On the more constructive side Siam is prosperous, their budget is balanced, their
gold reserve is 100% of paper currency outstanding. The people have plenty of food
and there seems little danger of Communism from within. A large group of American
officers are training the Thai (Sian) army and air force but most seem to feel that
Siam will put up little resistance should the Chinese Communists sweep through
Indo China and overrun the country. They individually seem to share the view held
by many of China's Nationalist soldiers that if your country is any good its worth
living for. We plan to spend this Friday afternoon Saturday end Sunday in Hongkong
then on Monday take off for Tokyo.
later - Iokyo - Tuesday, October 21st.
We had a wonderful time in Hongkong. Max Polin, George Sellett and Jerry 0'Donnell
met us at the airport. We all went to a cocktail party given by a prominent
Chinese for an old China Hand named Neil Starr and there met many old friends
including lots of refugees from Shanghai. Later we had dinner at Jerry's home high
up on the hills overlooking Repulse Bay. The next day Saturday, October 18th,
we did some shopping, called on old friends and had dinner at a Chinese restaurant

specializing in squab served with a knife and fork. Sunday Max Polin drove
us up to the Peak and all around Hongkong Island to the Shekko Country Club
where Jerry and later George Sellett joined us for lunch. That night Mex Polin
gave a party at a Chinese Szrchuwan chow restaurant with all of our favorite
dishes. He invited some old friends from Shanghai - the Henningsons as well as
George Sellett, Jerry and Mr. and Mrs. Al Lewis who are with PAA at Mieni and are
on a trip around the World. We had lots of fun and lots of gombeis ("Bottoms-up"
to most of you with Chinese rice wine
or Shao Shing.
Monday Debby did some more shopping and believe it or not bought some baskets. The
weather was 100% perfect in Hongkong. We stayed at the Penninsula Hotel on the
Kowloon or mainland side and our room on the 4th floor faced toward the Bay. We
spent a lot of time especially at dusk watching the junks and other water traffic
plying that magnificient harbor with the lights coming on up and down the mountair
which form the City of Victoria. It is without doubt one of the great sights -
one of the modern seven wonders of the world is Hongkong. We were amazed at the di
amount of building - apartments, hotels, seven new motion picture houses, stores
and residences abuilding all over Kowloon and Hongkong. Certainly there is little
fear of a Communist sweep so far as the Colony is concerned. An interesting fact
is that on October 10th (the Chinese 4th of July) there were ten times as many
Nationalist flags flying in Hongkong as there were Red hammer and sickle whereas
last year it was just the fevefse. That may mean something.
Our best to all of you.
1.M.B.
